paragraphs.heading: The black hole at our center
paragraphs.text: Sagittarius A*, shortened to Sgr A*, is the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. Seen from Earth, it lies near the border of the constellations Sagittarius and Scorpius. It is a bright and very compact source of radio waves. The black hole itself cannot be seen, because light cannot escape its gravity, so astronomers can only watch nearby things it affects. The radio and infrared energy we pick up comes from gas and dust heated to millions of degrees as it falls in.

paragraphs.heading: Finding it
paragraphs.text: In April 1933 Karl Jansky detected a radio signal coming from the direction of Sagittarius, toward the galaxy's center, and that source became known as Sagittarius A. Later work showed Sagittarius A is made of several overlapping parts. Bruce Balick and Robert Brown found its bright, very compact part on 13 and 15 February 1974, using an interferometer of the National Radio Astronomy Observatory. Brown named it Sgr A* in a 1982 paper because the source was "exciting", and excited states of atoms are marked with an asterisk.

paragraphs.heading: Weighing it with stars
paragraphs.text: Astronomers measured it using stars that orbit it, especially the star S2. In 1994 a Berkeley team that included Charles Townes and Reinhard Genzel showed that the mass at Sgr A* was tightly packed and around 3 million Suns. In 2002 a team led by Genzel reported ten years of watching S2 move near Sgr A*, and its orbit put about 4.1 million solar masses inside a radius of no more than 17 light-hours. Their analysis ruled out a cluster of dark stars there. The current best estimate of the mass is 4.297 million solar masses.

paragraphs.heading: A Nobel Prize
paragraphs.text: Genzel and Andrea Ghez each won a quarter of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for finding that Sgr A* is a supermassive compact object that only a black hole could explain. Roger Penrose received the other half, for showing that general relativity firmly predicts that black holes form.

paragraphs.heading: The first picture
paragraphs.text: On 12 May 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope, a worldwide network of radio observatories, released the first image of Sgr A*, showing the accretion disk around its event horizon. The image confirms the object contains a black hole, and it was the second black hole image, after the one in Messier 87 in 2019. The data were gathered in 2017 by eight observatories at six sites. Turning them into an image took five years of calculations, and the work was harder because the radio emission from Sgr A* changes within minutes.

paragraphs.heading: How big it looks
paragraphs.text: The image gives the source an overall angular size of about 51.8 microarcseconds. At a distance of 27,000 light-years, that works out to a diameter of 64.1 million kilometres, roughly 46 times the width of the Sun. Astronomers cannot see it in visible light, because dust and gas between it and Earth dim it by 25 magnitudes.
